title: pH change during the titration of a strong base with a strong acid
objective: Follow the pH of a strong base as standard acid is run in from a burette
Identify the steep jump in pH near the equivalence point
Relate the mid-point of the jump to the equivalence volume found by N1V1=N2V2
Explain why an indicator's colour-change range must straddle this jump

theory.statement: As standard acid is added to a strong base, the pH falls only slowly at first (the base is in large excess), then falls very steeply over a tiny volume near the equivalence point, before levelling off again in the acidic region. A universal indicator lets the whole curve be followed by colour, from violet through green to red.
theory.derivationNote: For a strong base neutralised by a strong acid, [OH-] before equivalence is set by the excess base, [H+] after equivalence by the excess acid, and at equivalence the solution is exactly neutral (pH 7 at 298 K) because neither ion left in solution hydrolyses. The steepness of the jump follows from pH being a LOGARITHMIC measure: near equivalence, a very small volume of acid changes the H+/OH- concentration by orders of magnitude.
keyEquations: At the equivalence point of a strong acid/strong base titration, pH = 7 (298 K)
N1V1 = N2V2 locates the equivalence volume

apparatus.name: Burette
apparatus.why: Delivers the standard acid in small, measured increments

apparatus.name: Conical flask
apparatus.why: Holds the base solution being titrated

apparatus.name: Universal indicator solution
apparatus.why: Gives a continuous colour scale across the whole pH range, unlike a single-colour-change indicator

apparatus.name: pH colour chart
apparatus.why: Converts the observed colour to an approximate pH

apparatus.name: Standard HCl
apparatus.why: The titrant of accurately known concentration

procedure.text: Fill the burette with standard HCl and note the initial reading.
Pipette 20 mL of the NaOH solution into a conical flask and add a few drops of universal indicator.
Add acid in 1 mL portions, swirling and noting the colour (and approximate pH) after each addition.
As the colour begins to change rapidly, add the acid in single drops.
Continue a little past the point where the colour stops changing rapidly, to see the curve level off again.
Plot pH against the volume of acid added, and locate the steepest part of the curve.

steps: Record pH at increasing volumes of acid added
Identify the volume at which pH changes most steeply per mL

expectedResult.quantity: Volume of acid at the steepest part of the curve (equivalence)
expectedResult.statement: The pH falls slowly at first, plunges steeply through pH 7 near 19.5-20 mL of acid added, then levels off in the acidic region — the equivalence point located graphically agrees with N1V1=N2V2.

safety: Universal indicator and dilute acids are of low hazard, but avoid contact with eyes.
Handle the burette over a tray in case of drips.
sourcesOfError: Reading the colour chart is subjective, especially in the green/yellow-green region.
Adding acid too fast near the jump can overshoot the steepest region entirely.
A stale or wrongly-prepared universal indicator gives misleading colours.

viva.question: Why is the pH change near the equivalence point so much steeper than elsewhere on the curve?
viva.expectedConcept: pH is a logarithmic scale. Near equivalence, both [H+] and [OH-] are very small and nearly equal, so a tiny addition of acid changes their ratio, and hence the logarithm, by a large amount.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the acid reacts unusually fast near equivalence.

viva.question: What is the pH at the equivalence point of this titration, and why?
viva.expectedConcept: About 7, because the salt formed (NaCl) is from a strong acid and a strong base and does not hydrolyse.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming every titration's equivalence point is at pH 7.

viva.question: Why must an indicator's colour-change range fall within the steep part of the curve?
viva.expectedConcept: Only there does a single drop of titrant produce a large, sharp colour change; elsewhere the colour would change gradually over many mL, giving an imprecise end point.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing any indicator works for any titration.

preLab.question: At the equivalence point of NaOH titrated with HCl, the pH is closest to:
preLab.feedback: Both ions of the salt formed, Na+ and Cl-, are spectators that do not hydrolyse, so the solution is neutral.

duringLab.question: Record at least six readings, closely spaced near the jump.

postLab.question: At what volume (mL) does the pH change most steeply?
postLab.feedback: Close to the stoichiometric volume, about 19.5-20 mL for these concentrations.

assumptions: Indicator equilibrium is fast compared with mixing
edgeCases: A weak acid or base would shift the equivalence pH away from 7
expectedBehaviour: S-shaped curve with pH 7 at the steepest point
